summary: This standards-track RFC outlines the audio codec and processing requirements for WebRTC endpoints.

eli5.summary: The minimum sound formats and processing every browser calling tool must support so they can talk to each other.

questions: which audio codecs must webrtc support
what audio level does webrtc use
subtitle: The minimum audio codecs and sound handling every WebRTC endpoint must support so browser calls can interoperate.

tldr.problem: WebRTC applications from different vendors need to exchange voice and be able to talk to each other without converting audio from one format to another.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC requires every endpoint to implement Opus, G.711 (PCMA and PCMU), comfort noise and DTMF telephone events, and gives guidance on audio level and echo cancellation.
tldr.outcome: Any two WebRTC endpoints share a baseline set of codecs, and the G.711 requirement gives voice interoperability with legacy phone systems.

today: RFC 7874 is a Proposed Standard from May 2016. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it points to RFC 7875 for additional codecs.

sections.title: Why Baseline Audio Rules
sections.content:
The success of Web Real-Time Communications (WebRTC) depends on voice and video interoperability between WebRTC applications. RFC 7874 covers the audio half: which codecs an endpoint has to implement and how it should handle audio levels and echo.

The document uses the RFC 2119 key words, so MUST and REQUIRED mark hard requirements while SHOULD and RECOMMENDED mark strong advice.
sections.eli5: Before a group call can work, everyone has to agree on some basic rules for sound. This RFC writes those rules down.

sections.title: Required Codecs
sections.content:
WebRTC endpoints are REQUIRED to implement Opus (RFC 6716) with the payload format from RFC 7587, and PCMA and PCMU (ITU-T G.711) with the payload format in Section 4.5.14 of RFC 3551.

If an endpoint has other suitable audio codecs, it is RECOMMENDED that it include them in the offer too, which makes it more likely that a session can be set up without transcoding the audio.

When an endpoint can process audio at a sampling rate higher than 8 kHz, it is RECOMMENDED that Opus be offered before PCMA/PCMU. All Opus modes MUST be supported on the decoder side. The choice of encoder-side modes is left to the implementer, and endpoints MAY use offer/answer to signal a preference for a particular mode or ptime.

Codecs beyond the mandatory ones are covered in RFC 7875.
sections.eli5: Everybody must know two common ways of squishing sound for sending, one modern and one old. Offering the better one first gives the best sound.

sections.title: Comfort Noise and DTMF Events
sections.content:
Endpoints MUST support RFC 3389 comfort noise (CN) for streams encoded with G.711 or any other supported codec that has no comfort noise of its own. Opus provides its own mechanism, so using RFC 3389 CN with Opus is NOT RECOMMENDED. Senders may use Discontinuous Transmission (DTX) and CN, but it is OPTIONAL.

Endpoints are also REQUIRED to support the audio/telephone-event media type from RFC 4733. They MAY send DTMF events at any time and SHOULD suppress in-band DTMF tones. Each event MUST last no more than 8000 ms and no less than 40 ms, with a recommended default of 100 ms. The gap between events MUST be at least 30 ms, with a recommended default of 70 ms.

Endpoints must be able to generate and consume event codes 0 to 15, which cover the digits 0 to 9, the star and pound keys, and A to D. They do not have to do anything with received tones except drop them gracefully, and there is no API to tell JavaScript about received DTMF.
sections.eli5: Comfort noise is soft background hiss played during silence so the line does not feel dead. Phone keypad beeps are sent as little messages instead of real sounds.

sections.title: Audio Level
sections.content:
The RFC wants a standard on-the-wire speech level, so users do not have to adjust playback by hand and conference mixing is easier. It aims for the active audio level of -19 dBm0 recommended by ITU-T G.169 and G.115. WebRTC audio can be sampled anywhere from 8 to 48 kHz and higher, so the level SHOULD be measured by considering only frequencies above 300 Hz. The RECOMMENDED filter is a second-order Butterworth filter with a 300 Hz cutoff. The level SHOULD also be adapted to avoid clipping, either by lowering the gain below -19 dBm0 or by using a compressor.

For linear 16-bit PCM with values of +/-32767, -19 dBm0 is an RMS level of 2600, counting only active speech.

  • If the endpoint controls the whole capture path (like a regular phone), the gain is RECOMMENDED to be set so an average speaker reaches 2600.
  • If it does not (like a software endpoint), it SHOULD use automatic gain control (AGC) to hold the level at 2600 +/- 6 dB.
  • For music or desktop sharing, the level SHOULD NOT be adjusted automatically and the user should be able to set the gain by hand.

Some devices calibrate output for commercial music, which is typically around 12 dB louder than this level, so endpoints MAY increase gain before playback.
sections.eli5: Everyone should talk at about the same loudness, like a classroom where nobody whispers and nobody shouts. A helper turns the volume up or down automatically when needed.

sections.title: Acoustic Echo Cancellation
sections.content:
The RFC expects people to use WebRTC on notebook computers with a built-in microphone and speakers, which makes echo a hard problem. It does not mandate a specific algorithm, but says echo cancellation improves the user experience and should be implemented.

Endpoints SHOULD include an AEC or some other form of echo control. On general-purpose platforms, capture and playback may use different clocks, for example a webcam for capture and a separate soundcard for playback, so their sampling rates are likely to differ slightly. Endpoint AECs SHOULD be robust to this unless they ship with hardware that samples both from the same clock.

Endpoints SHOULD let the whole AEC or its nonlinear processing (NLP) be turned off for uses such as music, and SHOULD be able to detect a headset and disable echo cancellation. A local far-end echo canceller MAY be included for remote endpoints that lack one, but SHOULD then be disabled by default.
sections.eli5: Echo happens when your speakers' sound goes back into your microphone. Echo cancellation is like a friend who hushes the repeat, but it should switch off when you wear headphones.

sections.title: Legacy Phone Interoperability
sections.content: The codec requirements ensure, at a minimum, voice interoperability between WebRTC endpoints and legacy phone systems that support G.711. That is the reason PCMA and PCMU are on the mandatory list alongside Opus.
sections.eli5: Because everyone must also know the old phone language, new web calls can still talk to old telephones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security concerns about the codecs themselves are left to their own specifications: RFC 6716, RFC 7587, RFC 3551, RFC 3389 and RFC 4733. RTP-based concerns come from the RTP base specification.

Following the guidelines in RFC 6562, implementers should decide whether variable bitrate is appropriate for their application. Encryption and authentication are beyond the scope of this document.
sections.eli5: This RFC does not lock the doors itself. It points to other documents for that, and warns that changing how much data is sent can leak hints about what is being said.

items.title: Opus
items.text: Required, with the RFC 7587 payload format; offered first above 8 kHz.

items.title: PCMA and PCMU
items.text: G.711 codecs, required for legacy phone interoperability.

items.title: Comfort noise
items.text: RFC 3389 CN for codecs without their own; not recommended with Opus.

items.title: Telephone events
items.text: DTMF digits as RFC 4733 events, codes 0 to 15.
